hints: Recall that the graph of $y = f^{-1}(x)$ is the reflection of $y = f(x)$ in the line $y = x$.
Draw the reflected curve starting at $(3, 0)$ and ending at $(5, 2\pi)$.
walkthrough:
Reflect key endpoints and intersections of $y = f(x)$ in the diagonal mirror line $y = x$:
$$\text{Endpoint } (0, 3) \longrightarrow (3, 0)$$
$$\text{Endpoint } (2\pi, 5) \longrightarrow (5, 2\pi)$$
$$\text{Intersection with } y = x \text{ remains invariant}$$
Sketch the reflected curve $y = f^{-1}(x)$ starting from $(3, 0)$ on the $x$-axis and rising smoothly to $(5, 2\pi)$.

hints: Set $y = 3 + 2\sin(\frac{1}{4}x)$ and isolate the sine term: $\sin(\frac{1}{4}x) = \frac{y-3}{2}$.
Take the inverse sine of both sides: $\frac{1}{4}x = \sin^{-1}\left(\frac{y-3}{2}\right)$.
Multiply by $4$ and interchange variables to write $f^{-1}(x)$.
walkthrough:
Set $y = f(x)$ and isolate the trigonometric term:
$$y = 3 + 2\sin\left(\frac{1}{4}x\right) \implies 2\sin\left(\frac{1}{4}x\right) = y - 3 \implies \sin\left(\frac{1}{4}x\right) = \frac{y - 3}{2}$$

Apply the inverse sine function to solve for $\frac{1}{4}x$:
$$\frac{1}{4}x = \sin^{-1}\left(\frac{y - 3}{2}\right)$$

Multiply both sides by $4$ and swap variables to state $f^{-1}(x)$:
$$f^{-1}(x) = 4\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{x - 3}{2}\right)$$

hints: Extend the curve for negative $x$ down to $x = -2\pi$, where $g(-2\pi) = 3 + 2\sin(-\pi/2) = 1$.
Check whether the resulting graph over $[-2\pi, 2\pi]$ is strictly increasing and passes the horizontal line test.
Conclude whether $g$ is a one-to-one function and therefore has an inverse.
walkthrough:
Continue the graph of $g(x) = 3 + 2\sin\left(\frac{1}{4}x\right)$ to the left for $-2\pi \le x \le 0$:
$$\text{At } x = -2\pi: \quad g(-2\pi) = 3 + 2\sin\left(-\frac{\pi}{2}\right) = 3 - 2 = 1$$
Observe that the function $g(x)$ is strictly increasing across the entire domain $[-2\pi, 2\pi]$, with no turning points.
Because the function is strictly increasing, it is one-to-one (passes the horizontal line test), and therefore $g$ has an inverse.

hints: Identify the horizontal transformation from $\sin x$ to $\sin\left(\frac{1}{4}x\right)$: a stretch parallel to the $x$-axis with scale factor $4$.
Identify the vertical scaling from $\sin\left(\frac{1}{4}x\right)$ to $2\sin\left(\frac{1}{4}x\right)$: a stretch parallel to the $y$-axis with scale factor $2$.
Identify the vertical shift from $2\sin\left(\frac{1}{4}x\right)$ to $3 + 2\sin\left(\frac{1}{4}x\right)$: a translation by vector $\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}$.
Ensure the vertical stretch is applied before the vertical translation.
walkthrough:
Compare $y = \sin x$ to $y = 3 + 2\sin\left(\frac{1}{4}x\right)$ step by step in order:
$$1.\ \text{Stretch parallel to the } x\text{-axis (or in the } x\text{-direction) with scale factor } 4$$
$$\text{mapping } y = \sin x \longrightarrow y = \sin\left(\frac{1}{4}x\right)$$

Apply the vertical scaling:
$$2.\ \text{Stretch parallel to the } y\text{-axis (or in the } y\text{-direction) with scale factor } 2$$
$$\text{mapping } y = \sin\left(\frac{1}{4}x\right) \longrightarrow y = 2\sin\left(\frac{1}{4}x\right)$$

Apply the vertical shift:
$$3.\ \text{Translation by vector } \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix} \text{ (or } 3 \text{ units vertically upwards)}$$
$$\text{mapping } y = 2\sin\left(\frac{1}{4}x\right) \longrightarrow y = 3 + 2\sin\left(\frac{1}{4}x\right)$$
$$\text{(Note: The horizontal stretch may occur anywhere, but the vertical stretch must precede the translation.)}$$
